play.title: Dispatch desk
play.missionText: The “orders” topic has 3 partitions — three belts. Send orders and find out where each one lands.

objectives.noKey: Send an order with no key
objectives.allBelts: Get a parcel onto every belt

send5.title: Offsets only go up
send5.body: Each belt stamps parcels 0, 1, 2… in arrival order. That number is the offset — its position in this partition's log.

sameKey.title: Same key → same partition
sameKey.body: murmur2(key) % partitions always gives the same belt for the same key. That's how Kafka keeps one customer's orders in order.

noKey.title: No key? Sticky partition
noKey.body: Records without a key stick to one belt until a batch fills, then switch. Fast — but no ordering guarantee across them.

allBelts.title: Partitions spread the load
allBelts.body: Different keys land on different belts, so work runs in parallel. Order is only guaranteed inside one partition.

complete.title: Shift complete!
complete.body: You've got keys, partitions and offsets. Keep dispatching — World 1 opens soon.

w1.title: Events & the Log
w1.body: Every story in Kafka starts with a record on a log. Learn what a record is, why reading never deletes, what offsets are and how topics organize it all.

w2.title: Partitions & Keys
w2.body: Partitions are how Kafka scales, and keys are how it keeps order. Learn how to choose a partition count, why keys matter and what happens when you add partitions later.

w3.title: Producers
w3.body: How records leave the producer: batching and linger, compression, the acks that decide when a write counts as saved, and the idempotence that stops retries from creating duplicates.

w4.title: Consumers & Groups
w4.body: The reading side: the poll loop, consumer groups that share partitions, rebalances (and how to avoid stopping the line), committed offsets, and the lag that tells you if you’re keeping up.

sandbox.title: Free dispatch
sandbox.body: No goals, no quiz: just you, three conveyors and your customers.

w5.title: Brokers & Replication
w5.body: How a cluster survives failures: replicas, leaders and followers, the ISR and high watermark, min.insync.replicas, and the KRaft controllers that run elections.

shift.title: Morning shift
shift.empty: Finish a level to get your first review.
shift.due: {n, plural, one {# concept} other {# concepts}} ready for review

w6.title: Delivery guarantees
w6.body: At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once: diagnose real symptoms, then use transactions so a group of writes happens all together or not at all.

w7.title: Retention & Compaction
w7.body: Where old data goes: log segments, retention that deletes whole segments, compaction that keeps the latest value per key, and tiered storage that moves history to cheap remote storage.

map.soonBody: This island is still under construction. More Kafka is on the way.

w8.title: Streams & Connect
w8.body: Kafka beyond the brokers: Connect pipes data in and out, and Kafka Streams turns topics into tables, counts that survive crashes, and time windows.

w9.title: Queues & Performance
w9.body: Share groups turn Kafka into a work queue with locks and retries. Then: why Kafka is so fast, what TLS costs, and quotas that tame noisy clients.

1-1.title: First parcel
1-1.summary: What's inside a Kafka record: key, value, headers and timestamp.

brief.title: Every event is a parcel
brief.body: Something happened (alice placed an order) and the shop wants the world to know. In Kafka that fact travels as a record. Here, each record is a parcel on its way through the hub.
brief.breaks: a real parcel can be opened and repacked. A Kafka record can’t: once it’s written, it is immutable.

pack.title: Pack your first order
pack.body: Pick a customer: their name becomes the record’s key. Toggle a header if you like, then watch the parcel leave the producer.
pack.success: Your first record is on the log!

which.q: Which part of the record decides which conveyor (partition) it goes to?
which.why: The partitioner hashes the key: murmur2(key) % partitions. Value, headers and timestamp don’t affect where it goes.

again.q: dave just landed on P{p}. Send dave again: which conveyor?
again.why: Same key, same hash, same partition: P{p}. That’s how all of one customer’s records stay in order.

more.title: Three more, one without a key
more.body: Send 3 more orders, and make at least one of them without a key. Watch where the keyless ones go.
more.success: Records without a key use sticky partitioning: they fill one conveyor for a while, then switch.

notPart.q: Which of these is NOT part of a Kafka record?
notPart.consumer: The consumer that will read it
notPart.why: A record has a key, a value, headers and a timestamp. It doesn’t know who will read it: any number of consumers can.

bytes.q: To the broker, a record’s value is…
bytes.why: Brokers store and serve bytes. Turning them into JSON, Avro or objects is the clients’ job (serializers).

timestamp.q: With the default setting (CreateTime), who sets a record’s timestamp?
timestamp.why: message.timestamp.type=CreateTime is the default: the producer stamps it. With LogAppendTime the broker does.

nullKey.q: Can a record be sent with a null key?
nullKey.yes: Yes, it’s spread with sticky partitioning
nullKey.why: Keys are optional. Keyless records stick to one partition until a batch fills, then move on, so there’s no per-key ordering.

1-2.title: The belt never forgets
1-2.summary: Reading doesn’t delete: consumers keep a position, and records are immutable.

brief.title: Reading isn’t taking
brief.body: Two teams need the orders: Billing charges customers and Shipping sends boxes. Each one is a consumer group, a robot arm that scans parcels and remembers how far it has read.
brief.breaks: in a warehouse, picking up a parcel removes it. In Kafka, reading only copies the data: the parcel stays on the belt for everyone else.

arrive.title: Orders arrive
arrive.body: The shop sends four orders to the orders topic. Both arms are waiting at offset 0.

read.q: Billing reads the record at offset 0. What happens to that parcel?
read.moves: It moves to the end of the belt
read.why: It stays exactly where it is. Billing’s flag moves to offset 1: that’s its position, the next record it will read.

catch.title: Let Shipping catch up
catch.body: Use the buttons to make Shipping read the first 3 orders. Billing’s position doesn’t change: each group keeps its own.
catch.success: Two groups, same records, independent positions.

count.q: Billing is at position {billing} and Shipping at {shipping}. How many parcels are still on the belt?
count.why: All {n} of them. Reading never deletes. Records leave the log only when retention removes old ones, which is a story for later.

change.title: Changing your mind
change.body: alice wants to change her order. You might want to edit the parcel at offset 0, but the log is append-only: records can’t be edited or moved.
change.note: to “update”, you append a new record with the same key. Consumers see both, in order, and the newest one wins.

update.q: alice changes her order. What do you do?
update.append: Append a new record with key alice
update.why: Append a new record. The old one stays, and both keep their offsets. Kafka is a history of facts, not a table you overwrite.

remain.q: A partition holds {n} records. Group Billing has read all of them. How many records are still in the partition?
remain.why: Still {n}. Reading moves the group’s position. It never removes records.

left.q: A partition has offsets 0 to {last}. Shipping’s position is {p}. How many records does Shipping still have to read?
left.why: The log holds {n} records (0…{last}). Position {p} means offsets 0…{p}−1 are done, so {left} remain.

groups.q: Two consumer groups read the same topic. Their positions are…
groups.independent: Independent: each group has its own
groups.shared: Shared: one position for the topic
groups.why: Each group tracks its own position, so many teams can read the same data at their own pace.

update.q: How do you “update” a record in Kafka?
update.append: Append a new record with the same key
update.replace: Delete it and insert at the same offset
update.why: The log is append-only and records are immutable. A new record with the same key carries the update.

1-3.title: Stamps
1-3.summary: Offsets: every partition numbers its records 0, 1, 2… on its own.

brief.title: The stamp is the offset
brief.body: When a parcel lands, its conveyor stamps it with the next number. That number is the offset: its permanent position in that partition’s log.
brief.breaks: a counter can be reset. Offsets never are. Even after old records are deleted, their numbers are never reused.

warm.title: Warming up
warm.body: Five orders roll in. Watch the stamps: each conveyor counts on its own.

nextOffset.q: {key} goes to P{p}, which already holds {c} parcels. What offset will it get?
nextOffset.why: Offsets start at 0, so a partition with {c} records has used 0…{c}−1. The next one is {c}, the log-end offset.

where.q: bob already has parcels on the line. Where will bob’s next parcel land?
where.why: Same key, same partition: P{p}. You don’t need to compute murmur2, you just need to remember where the key went before.

own.q: What offset will the next parcel on P{q} get? (It’s {key}’s conveyor.)
own.why: P{q} has its own counter: its next offset is {n}, whatever the other conveyors are at.

fill.title: Fill P1 to offset 4
fill.body: Get P1 to 5 parcels (offsets 0–4). Which customers land on P1? Experiment. You can also type any key you like.
fill.success: You found P1’s keys. Notice: P1’s offsets don’t care what P0 or P2 are doing.

last.q: P0’s next offset is {n}. You send {k} records to P0. What offset does the last one get?
last.why: They get {n}, {n}+1, … so the last is {n} + {k} − 1 = {last}.

unique.why: Every partition counts from 0, so P0 offset 3 and P1 offset 3 are different records. Offset + partition (+ topic) identify a record.

count.q: A partition holds offsets 0 to {m}. How many records is that?

position.next: The offset of the next record it will read
position.last: The offset of the last record it read
position.deleted: How many records it has deleted
position.why: Position = next offset to read. A consumer at position 5 has processed offsets 0–4.

1-4.title: Sorting docks
1-4.summary: Topics: named logs that keep different kinds of events apart.

brief.title: Each line is a topic
brief.body: The hub now handles two kinds of events: orders and payments. Each kind gets its own production line, a topic, with its own name and its own conveyors (partitions).
brief.breaks: a topic isn’t a queue. Reading doesn’t empty it, and many groups can read it at once.

route.title: Route the events
route.body: Events arrive one by one. Send each one to the right topic: orders to orders, payments to payments. Get 6 right.
route.success: Sorted! Producers always say which topic a record goes to.

cross.q: alice has an order (in orders) and a payment (in payments). Is the order between those two records guaranteed?
cross.no: No: ordering is only per partition, and these are different topics
cross.yes: Yes: they have the same key
cross.why: Kafka guarantees order within a partition. Different topics are different logs, so there’s no ordering between them, even for the same key.

cli.title: Creating a topic, for real
cli.body: Everything you’ve seen maps to real commands. This creates the payments topic with 2 partitions on a local broker. Replication comes in World 5.

count.q: How many conveyors (partitions) will this topic have?

what.log: A named log, split into partitions
what.queue: A single queue that empties as you read
what.why: A topic is a named, append-only log split into partitions. It keeps records after they’re read.

cli.q: How many partitions will this topic have?

after.q: After a consumer group reads a record from a topic, the record…
after.why: Reading never deletes. Records stay until retention (default 7 days) or compaction removes them.

order.q: Kafka guarantees the order of records…
order.why: Only within a partition. That’s why keys matter: the same key always goes to the same partition.

2-1.title: Traffic jam
2-1.summary: Partitions are the unit of parallelism: more conveyors, more workers.

brief.title: Black Friday rush
brief.body: Orders are pouring in, 2 per second. The fulfilment robot packs 1 per second per conveyor, and the orders topic has just one conveyor. Can you keep up?
brief.breaks: in Kafka you can add partitions to a live topic, but you can never remove them.

rush.title: Keep the backlog down
rush.body: Orders arrive on their own. Add conveyors until the backlog stays at 3 or less for 5 seconds.
rush.success: Backlog under control! Each new partition gave the robot one more lane to work on in parallel.

unit.title: Partitions are lanes of work
unit.body: Within a consumer group, each partition is read by at most one consumer at a time. So the partition count caps how many consumers can work in parallel. Pick it for the throughput you’ll need later, because shrinking isn’t possible.

map.consumer: One consumer per partition (in a group)

min.q: Orders arrive at {rate} per second. Each worker packs 1 per second, one worker per partition. What’s the minimum number of partitions?
min.why: {rate} records/s ÷ 1 record/s per partition = {rate} partitions. Teams usually add headroom on top.

reduce.q: Can you shrink the topic from 4 partitions back to 2?
reduce.no: No: partitions can only be added
reduce.empty: Only if the topic is empty
reduce.why: Kafka can only add partitions. To get fewer, you create a new topic and migrate to it.

maxConsumers.q: A topic has {n} partitions. At most how many consumers in ONE group can read it in parallel?
maxConsumers.why: {n}: each partition goes to one consumer in the group. Any extra consumers sit idle.

capacity.q: Producers write {p} records/s. One consumer handles {c} records/s. What’s the minimum number of partitions to keep up?
capacity.why: {p} ÷ {c} = {k} partitions, so {k} consumers can work in parallel.

unit.q: The unit of parallelism in Kafka is the…
unit.why: Partitions are what get spread across consumers (and brokers).

shrink.q: How do you lower a topic’s partition count?
shrink.cannot: You can’t: create a new topic and migrate
shrink.delete: Delete the last partitions one by one
shrink.why: Partition counts only go up. Plan ahead, or move to a new topic.

2-2.title: Same customer, same belt
2-2.summary: Keys keep each customer’s events in order.

brief.title: alice’s three orders
brief.body: alice ordered a phone (#1), then a case (#2), then cancelled the case (#3). They must be handled in that order. Today the producer ignores keys and deals records round-robin across the conveyors.

busy.title: P0 is busy
busy.body: A bulk import just dumped a pile of parcels onto P0. The robot works through each conveyor at the same pace.

rr.title: Send alice’s 3 orders
rr.body: Press the button three times and watch the Delivered list. In what order does alice’s stuff get handled?
rr.success: Uh-oh: #2 and #3 were handled before #1! Round-robin put them on different conveyors, and P0 was busy.

keys.title: The key keeps the order
keys.body: With a key, the partitioner sends every record of a customer to the same partition. One partition is read in order, so that customer’s events are handled in order, even when another conveyor is faster.
keys.breaks: order is only guaranteed per partition. Records with different keys on different partitions have no order between them.

keyed.title: Try again, with keys
keyed.body: Now carol sends 3 orders with her key. Watch the delivery list.

where.why: P{p}, like all of carol’s orders. Same key, same partition.

how.q: To keep each customer’s events in order, the producer should…
how.key: Use the customer id as the key
how.why: Same key → same partition → read in order.

rr.q: Records spread round-robin (or keyless) give you…
rr.why: They land on different partitions, which are read independently.

first.q: alice’s records sit at offsets {a}, {bb} and {c} of P1. Which offset does a consumer read first?
first.why: A partition is read in offset order: {a}, then {bb}, then {c}.

hot.q: One key gets 90% of all traffic. What happens?
hot.hotspot: Its partition becomes a hot spot
hot.why: All records of a key go to one partition, so one consumer gets swamped. That’s the hot key problem.

2-3.title: No label?
2-3.summary: Keyless records and the sticky partitioner.

brief.title: Keyless parcels ride together
brief.body: Not every event needs a key. With key = null, the default partitioner is sticky: it fills one partition’s batch, then moves to the next. Fewer, fuller batches mean fewer requests.
brief.breaks: real Kafka switches when the batch reaches batch.size bytes (16 KB by default). Here a batch is {bb} parcels so you can see it.

fill.title: Watch the batches
fill.body: Six keyless parcels roll in. Notice they don’t alternate: they stick.

next.q: Where will the next keyless parcel go?
next.why: P{p}: the sticky partitioner keeps filling the current batch (up to {bb} here) before switching.

why.q: Why stick to one partition instead of alternating on every record?
why.why: Sticky partitioning is a throughput optimization (KIP-794): full batches compress better and need fewer network round trips.

all.title: Fill every conveyor
all.body: Send keyless parcels until each conveyor has at least 4.
all.success: Even spread over time, and efficient batches along the way.

default.q: With the default partitioner, records with a null key are…
default.why: Keyless records stick to one partition per batch, then rotate.

count.q: Batches of {bb} records, {n} partitions, starting at P0. You send {k} keyless records. How many land on P0?
count.why: P0 gets each batch number 0, {n}, 2·{n}… Counting {k} records in batches of {bb}: {x} on P0.

why.why: Fuller batches mean fewer requests and better compression.

order.q: Do keyless records keep their order relative to each other?
order.partition: Only within the partition they land on
order.never: Never, not even within a partition
order.why: Order is per partition, so it holds only within each partition.

2-4.title: New belt, new chaos
2-4.summary: Adding partitions moves keys, and that breaks per-key ordering.

brief.title: The hub grows
brief.body: Business is booming and the team wants a 4th conveyor. Before pressing the button, remember what the partitioner computes: murmur2(key) % partitions.

before.title: Everyone in their place
before.body: Each customer sends an order. Note which conveyor each one uses.

same.q: After adding a 4th conveyor, will every customer still go to the same conveyor?
same.why: The divisor changed from 3 to 4, so hash % 4 differs from hash % 3 for many keys. Some stay, some move.

grow.title: Add the 4th conveyor
grow.body: Add P3, then send each customer again and spot who switched conveyors in the table.
grow.success: Some customers now live on a different conveyor, while their old orders stay where they were.

hurts.title: Why it hurts
hurts.body: Some of a customer’s old orders sit on one partition and the new ones on another. A consumer could handle the new ones first: per-key ordering broke at the resize.
hurts.breaks: plan partition counts up front. If you must grow a keyed topic, consider a new topic and a migration.

mod.q: A key’s (positive) hash is {h}. Which partition does it go to with 4 partitions?
A key’s (positive) hash is {h} and the topic has {n} partitions. Which partition?

risk.q: The main risk of adding partitions to a keyed topic is…
risk.ordering: Keys move, so per-key ordering breaks
risk.why: Existing records stay put, new ones may hash elsewhere, so a key’s history is split across partitions.

cmd.q: Which command adds partitions to a topic?
cmd.why: --alter --partitions raises the count. Reassign moves replicas between brokers.

old.moved: Are moved to the new partitions
old.why: Records are immutable and never move. Only new records use the new partition count.

3-1.title: Trucks wait or go
3-1.summary: Batching: batch.size and linger.ms trade latency for throughput.

brief.title: Every send is a trip
brief.body: Right now the producer ships every parcel on its own trip: one network request per record. Real producers group records per partition into batches. A batch leaves when it’s full (batch.size) or when it has waited linger.ms, whichever comes first.
brief.breaks: time is slowed down about 100× so you can see the trucks wait. Real linger.ms defaults to 5 ms (since Kafka 4.0), and batch.size is counted in bytes (16 KB), not parcels.

tune.title: Fewer trips, still fast
tune.body: Orders arrive 6 per second. Tune the two dials until you send ≤ 2.2 requests per second while parcels wait ≤ 700 ms on average, and hold it for 5 seconds.
tune.success: Fewer, fuller batches: less network chatter and only a little extra latency. That’s the batching trade-off.

when.q: batch.size = 4 parcels, linger.ms = 1000 ms, and parcels arrive at P0 one per second. After how many seconds does the first batch leave?
when.why: linger.ms runs out after 1 s, before the 4th parcel would arrive, so a partial batch leaves at second 1. Whichever limit comes first wins.

raise.why: Waiting a bit longer fills batches (better throughput and compression) at the cost of a little delay per record.

first.q: batch.size = {bb} records, records arrive every {ms} ms to one partition, linger.ms = {L} ms. How many records does the first batch hold?
first.why: The batch closes when it’s full ({bb}) or when linger.ms expires ({L} ms, by which time 1 + {L}/{ms} records could have arrived). Here that’s {count}.

linger.wait: How long to wait for more records before sending a batch
linger.retry: How long to wait between retries
linger.keep: How long records stay on the broker
linger.why: It’s a deliberate small delay so more records can join the batch.

default.q: What’s the default linger.ms in Kafka 4.x?
default.why: KIP-1030 changed it from 0 to 5 ms in Kafka 4.0, a small wait that improves batching.

bigger.tradeoff: Fewer requests and higher throughput, but more latency
bigger.why: Batching trades a little latency for a lot of efficiency.

3-2.title: Vacuum pack
3-2.summary: Compression: whole batches squeezed with gzip, snappy, lz4 or zstd.

brief.title: Squeeze the batch
brief.body: The network between the hub and the brokers is a narrow pipe. Producers can compress each batch before sending it. The broker stores it compressed, and the consumer unpacks it at the end.
brief.breaks: the ratios here are illustrative. Real compression depends on your data: repetitive JSON squeezes a lot, already-compressed images barely at all.

pipe.title: Fit through the pipe
pipe.body: 6 orders per second of 1 KB each, but the pipe only takes {cap} KB/s. Pick a codec that fits and watch the CPU cost.
pipe.success: It fits! Each codec trades CPU for size: zstd and gzip squeeze the most, lz4 and snappy are the fastest.

where.q: Where are the records finally decompressed?
where.why: The batch travels compressed end to end. The broker keeps it as the producer packed it (topic compression.type=producer), and the consumer decompresses.

best.why: More similar records in one batch means more repetition to squeeze. Batching and compression work together.

default.why: Compression is off by default. You opt in with compression.type.

unit.why: Compression applies to the whole batch, which is why bigger batches compress better.

broker.keeps: Stores the batch as the producer compressed it
broker.why: producer (the default) keeps whatever codec the producer used. No recompression.

wire.q: {rate} records/s of {kb} KB each, compressed to {pct}% of their size. How many KB/s go over the network?

3-3.title: Signed receipts
3-3.summary: acks: when does a write count as saved? Crash the leader and find out.

brief.title: Who signs the receipt?
brief.body: Each partition is copied to several brokers: a leader that takes the writes, and followers that copy from it. The producer’s acks setting decides when it gets its receipt: 0 (don’t wait), 1 (the leader wrote it), all (every in-sync replica has it).
brief.breaks: followers copy over the network. Here a copy takes about a second, so you can see the gap that real clusters close in milliseconds.

crash1.title: Crash test with acks=1
crash1.body: The producer sends three orders with acks=1 and then the leader’s broker dies. Watch the receipts.

fix.q: Receipts said ✓ but orders were lost. Which setting would have prevented it?
fix.why: With acks=all the producer only gets its receipt once every in-sync replica has the record, so a leader crash can’t take an acknowledged record with it.

crash2.title: Crash test with acks=all
crash2.body: Broker 2 is the leader now. First set acks=all, send a few orders, wait for their ✓, then crash the leader again. No acknowledged order should be lost.
crash2.success: Every ✓ survived the crash. That’s why acks=all has been the default since Kafka 3.0.

alone.q: Only one replica is left. With acks=all and the default min.insync.replicas=1, a write…
alone.succeeds: Succeeds: the leader alone is “all in-sync replicas”
alone.why: “All” means all in-sync replicas, and with min.insync.replicas=1 one is enough. Production clusters use RF=3 with min.insync.replicas=2. More in World 5.

one.q: acks=1 means the producer gets its ack when…
one.leader: The leader has written the record
one.why: Only the leader’s write is confirmed. Followers may not have it yet.

default.q: What’s the default acks since Kafka 3.0?
default.why: acks=all, together with idempotence, became the default in Kafka 3.0.

lose.q: Which setting can lose an acknowledged record if the leader dies right after acking?
lose.why: With acks=1 the record may exist only on the dead leader. (acks=0 can lose records too, but the producer was never promised anything.)

zero.nowait: The producer doesn’t wait for any acknowledgement
zero.why: Fire and forget: fastest, with no guarantee the record was stored.

3-4.title: Lost receipt
3-4.summary: Retries create duplicates, and idempotence stops them.

brief.title: The receipt got lost
brief.body: The network is flaky today. The broker writes the parcel, but the “got it!” reply sometimes vanishes on the way back. The producer can’t tell the difference, so it retries.
brief.breaks: Kafka doesn’t retry a fixed number of times: it keeps retrying until delivery.timeout.ms (2 minutes by default) runs out.

flaky.title: Flaky network
flaky.body: Send orders until something weird shows up on the conveyor.
flaky.success: A duplicate! The same order is on the log twice: the first write worked, only its receipt was lost.

seals.title: Numbered seals
seals.body: With idempotence, every producer gets an id and numbers its records per partition (seq). If a retry arrives with a number the broker already wrote, the broker drops it. Order is kept too, with up to 5 requests in flight. It’s on by default since Kafka 3.0.

fix.title: Turn on idempotence
fix.body: Switch idempotence on and keep sending. Watch the partitioner reject the retried copies.
fix.success: Retries still happen, but the log stays clean: each order exactly once.

protects.producers: Two different producers sending the same order
protects.why: It dedups retries from one producer session. Consumer-side duplicates and cross-producer duplicates need other tools (World 6).

default.q: What’s the default enable.idempotence since Kafka 3.0?
default.why: On by default, together with acks=all.

detect.q: How does the broker spot a duplicate retry?
detect.why: Each producer numbers its records per partition. A repeated number is a retry.

eos.session: Only for writes from one producer session into Kafka
eos.why: It removes producer-retry duplicates. End-to-end exactly-once needs transactions and read_committed consumers.

bound.q: What limits how long the producer keeps retrying?
bound.why: retries defaults to MAX_INT. delivery.timeout.ms (120 s) is the real bound.

4-1.title: Pull, don’t push
4-1.summary: Consumers poll: they ask for records, in batches of up to max.poll.records.

brief.title: Robots pull, the hub doesn’t push
brief.body: Kafka never pushes records at a consumer. The consumer runs a poll loop: “anything after my position?”, then the broker hands back a batch, the consumer processes it and asks again. How many records come back per poll is capped by max.poll.records.
brief.breaks: a real poll also waits up to fetch.max.wait.ms (500 ms) for data, and max.poll.records defaults to 500. Here everything is small and slow so you can see it.

keep.title: Keep up with the orders
keep.body: Orders arrive 3 per second. Every poll costs a round trip, so fetching one record at a time wastes most of the robot’s day. Tune max.poll.records until the backlog stays at 4 or less for 5 seconds.
keep.success: Bigger polls, less overhead per record: the robot keeps up.

next.q: A consumer’s position is 2, max.poll.records = 3, and the log holds offsets 0–9. What’s the last offset the next poll returns?
next.why: It reads from its position: offsets 2, 3 and 4. The last one is 4, and the position moves to 5.

slow.q: Processing one poll’s records takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms (5 minutes). What happens?
slow.kicked: The consumer is kicked out of the group and its partitions are rebalanced
slow.why: Missing max.poll.interval.ms makes the group think the consumer is stuck: it leaves the group and its partitions move. Expect a rebalance and re-processing.

who.q: How do records get from the broker to a consumer?
who.pull: The consumer pulls them with poll()
who.why: Kafka is pull-based, so each consumer reads at its own pace.

default.why: Up to 500 records per poll() by default.

last.q: Position {pos}, max.poll.records = {max}, the log ends at offset {end}. What’s the last offset the next poll returns?

slow.q: A consumer takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms between polls. Then…
slow.kicked: It’s removed from the group and a rebalance happens
slow.why: The group assumes it’s stuck, so its partitions go to other members.

4-2.title: Crews
4-2.summary: Consumer groups share partitions: one owner per partition, extras sit idle.

brief.title: One crew, many robots
brief.body: Robots that do the same job form a consumer group. The group splits the partitions among its members: each partition goes to exactly one member, so work runs in parallel and no record is handled twice within the group.

map.assigned: The conveyors in front of it

hire.title: Give every conveyor its own robot
hire.body: One robot is running all 4 conveyors. Hire robots until each conveyor has its own. Watch how the partitions get reassigned every time someone joins.
hire.success: Four robots, four conveyors: maximum parallelism for this topic.

fifth.q: 4 conveyors, 4 robots. You hire a 5th robot. How many conveyors does it get?
fifth.why: None. A partition can’t be split within a group, so the 5th member sits idle (zzz) until someone leaves.

cooks.title: Too many cooks
cooks.body: Members beyond the partition count are idle, but not useless: they’re hot standbys that take over the moment another member dies. And a different group (say, Billing) gets all partitions again, independently.
cooks.breaks: in a warehouse, extra workers can share a conveyor. In Kafka, one partition has one reader per group, full stop.

range.q: The range assignor, 3 robots, 4 partitions. How many partitions does the first robot (C1) get?
range.why: 4 ÷ 3 = 1 each, with 1 left over that goes to the first member: C1 gets 2 (P0, P1), C2 gets P2, C3 gets P3.

idle.q: A topic has {n} partitions and a group has {c} consumers. How many consumers sit idle?
idle.why: {c} − {n} = {idle}. Each partition has exactly one owner per group.

rule.q: Within one consumer group, a partition is read by…
rule.one: Exactly one member at a time
rule.why: That’s how a group spreads the work without double-processing.

twoGroups.q: Groups “billing” and “shipping” both read the topic orders. Then…
twoGroups.split: They split the records between them
twoGroups.first: Only the first group gets them
twoGroups.why: Groups are independent: each one reads the whole topic with its own positions.

range.q: The range assignor, {c} consumers, {n} partitions. How many partitions does the first consumer get?
range.why: ⌈{n} ÷ {c}⌉ = {first}: the first members take the remainder.

4-3.title: New hire
4-3.summary: Rebalances: eager stops the line, cooperative and KIP-848 keep it moving.

brief.title: Rebalance!
brief.body: When a member joins, leaves or crashes, the group rebalances: partitions move to new owners. While a partition is moving, nobody reads it, so the conveyor pauses (⏸). How much stops depends on the protocol.

eager.title: The classic way
eager.body: Two robots share 4 conveyors with the classic eager protocol. A third robot is about to join…

paused.q: How many conveyors stopped during that eager rebalance?
paused.why: Eager rebalancing revokes every partition from every member, then hands them out again: stop the world, even for partitions that end up with the same owner.

protocols.title: Three ways to change shifts
protocols.body: Eager (classic): everyone stops. Cooperative (classic + CooperativeStickyAssignor): only partitions that actually move pause. KIP-848 (group.protocol=consumer): the broker computes the assignment and members reconcile incrementally, with no global barrier. Brokers support KIP-848 by default since 4.0, but consumers still default to classic.

smooth.title: Hire without stopping the line
smooth.body: Orders keep coming. Choose a protocol, then hire (or let go of) a robot while pausing at most 1 conveyor.
smooth.meter: Conveyors paused in the last rebalance
smooth.success: Smooth! Only the partition that changed hands paused, and everything else kept flowing.

default.q: Kafka 4.x consumers use which group protocol by default?
default.why: The broker side of KIP-848 is on by default since 4.0, but clients must opt in, and 4.3 warns that classic will be deprecated.

eager.q: In an eager rebalance, which partitions pause?
eager.all: All of them, for every member
eager.why: Eager revokes everything first, then reassigns.

coop.q: With cooperative rebalancing, which partitions pause?
coop.why: Incremental: members keep what they own and only moving partitions are revoked.

kip.q: Which consumer setting opts into the KIP-848 protocol?

static.q: Which setting lets a consumer restart quickly without triggering a rebalance?
static.why: Static membership keeps the member’s identity, so a quick restart within the session timeout doesn’t reshuffle partitions.

4-4.title: Bookmarks
4-4.summary: Committed offsets: where a restart resumes, and how commit timing decides duplicates or loss.

brief.title: Bookmarks
brief.body: A consumer’s position (▲) lives in its memory. If it crashes, that memory is gone. So consumers commit their progress to Kafka (the internal __consumer_offsets topic): a bookmark ⚑ with the offset of the next record to read. A replacement resumes from the bookmark.

crash1.title: Crash test: auto-commit
crash1.body: Billing auto-commits every 6 seconds. Let it work a little, crash the robot, then hire a new one and watch the counters.
crash1.success: Duplicates! The new robot resumed from the last bookmark, behind records the old one had already processed.

before.q: What if Billing committed BEFORE processing each poll instead?
before.lost: Records could be lost (committed but never processed)
before.why: Committing first moves the bookmark past records that are still in the robot’s hands. A crash then skips them forever: at-most-once.

safe.title: Commit after processing
safe.body: Pick the commit strategy that never loses a record, then crash and replace the robot again. Keep orders flowing until at least 6 are processed.
safe.success: Nothing lost. At worst a record gets processed twice, so make your processing idempotent. That’s at-least-once, the usual default.

audit.q: A brand-new group “audit” starts with the default auto.offset.reset. Does it see the orders already on the conveyors?
audit.no: No: it starts at the end (latest) and only sees new orders
audit.yes: Yes, it reads everything from offset 0
audit.why: auto.offset.reset applies only when a group has no committed offset, and its default is latest. Set it to earliest to replay history.

meaning.next: The next record to read after a restart is offset 42
meaning.last: Offset 42 was the last record processed
meaning.why: Committed offsets point at the next record to consume.

before.why: A crash after the commit but before processing skips those records.

reset.why: New groups start at the end unless you choose earliest.

where.q: Where does Kafka store committed offsets?
where.why: Commits are records in __consumer_offsets. (ZooKeeper is gone since Kafka 4.0.)

4-5.title: Boss: Rush hour
4-5.summary: Lag: watch it, read it and bring it down with the right lever.

brief.title: Rush hour
brief.body: Consumer lag = log-end offset − committed offset: how far behind the group is. It’s the number every Kafka team watches. Orders are about to surge.
brief.breaks: lag is a count of records, not time. 100 records of lag can be milliseconds or hours depending on how fast you process.

rush.title: Survive rush hour
rush.body: 6 orders per second. Each robot handles about 2 per second. Hire robots and add conveyors until the lag stays at 6 or less for 8 seconds. Think about which lever runs out first.
rush.success: You beat rush hour! You needed more robots, and to have more robots working you needed more partitions.

fourth.q: 3 partitions, 3 robots, and the lag still grows. Hiring a 4th robot alone…
fourth.idle: Does nothing: it sits idle without a partition
fourth.faster: Speeds everything up by a third
fourth.split: Splits a partition with another robot
fourth.why: Parallelism is capped by the partition count. You need a 4th partition (keyed topics: mind the key moves!) or faster processing.

levers.title: The levers
levers.body: To bring lag down: more consumers (up to the partition count), more partitions (plan ahead, because keys move), faster processing per record, or bigger polls to cut overhead. In the real world you read lag with this command:

lag.q: A partition’s log ends at offset {end} and the group’s committed offset is {committed}. What’s the lag?

idle.q: There are as many consumers as partitions. Adding one more consumer to the group…
idle.why: No partition is left for it.

means.behind: Consumers are falling behind the producers
means.why: Records arrive faster than the group commits progress. Nothing is lost, it’s just waiting.

size.q: Producers write {rate} records/s. One consumer handles {per} records/s. Minimum partitions (and consumers) to keep up?

brief.title: One partition, three warehouses
brief.body: A Kafka cluster is a group of brokers. Each partition is stored on replication.factor of them. One replica is the leader: it takes every write (and serves reads by default). The others are followers that keep fetching from it.
brief.breaks: default.replication.factor is 1, so a topic created without thinking has no copies at all. Production clusters use 3.

copy.title: Followers fetch
copy.body: Three orders go to the leader. Watch the followers copy each parcel from the leader’s conveyor.

where.q: Where does the producer send its writes?
where.why: Producers only write to the leader. Followers fetch from it, just like consumers do.

lose.title: Lose a warehouse, keep the data
lose.body: Send a couple of orders and wait for their ✓. Then crash broker 1, the leader.
lose.success: A follower took over as leader and every ✓ order is still there. That’s what replicas are for.

rf.q: With replication.factor = 3, how many brokers can fail before an acknowledged record (acks=all) is at risk?
rf.why: Two. One copy must survive: RF − 1 failures.

default.why: 1: no copies. Always set it explicitly (3 is typical).

writes.q: Which replica handles a partition’s writes?
writes.why: All writes go through the leader.

survive.q: replication.factor = {rf}. How many replica failures can a partition survive and still have a copy?

followers.q: How do followers get new records?
followers.fetch: They fetch them from the leader
followers.why: Followers replicate by fetching from the leader.

5-2.title: Keeping up
5-2.summary: The ISR and the high watermark.

brief.title: In sync or out
brief.body: Replicas that keep up with the leader form the ISR (in-sync replicas). One that falls behind for longer than replica.lag.time.max.ms is dropped from it. A record is committed once every ISR member has it, and the high watermark (HW) marks that point: consumers only read below it.
brief.breaks: the real lag limit is 30 seconds. Here it’s about 2.5 so you don’t have to wait.

slow.title: Slow down a follower
slow.body: Orders keep arriving. Press slow on broker 3 and watch it fall out of the ISR (orange tag). Then press fix and watch it catch up and rejoin.
slow.success: Out, then back in. The ISR changes all the time in real clusters, and the HW only moves as fast as the slowest in-sync replica.

wait.q: While broker 3 was out of the ISR, did acks=all writes wait for it?
wait.no: No: acks=all waits for the ISR, and it wasn’t in it
wait.yes: Yes, they waited for all 3 replicas
wait.why: “All” means all in-sync replicas. Dropping a slow follower keeps writes fast.

read.leader: Up to the end of the leader’s log
read.slowest: Up to the slowest replica, in sync or not
read.why: Only committed records (below the HW) are visible, so a consumer never sees something that a failover could undo.

isr.caught: The replicas currently caught up with the leader
isr.why: In-sync replicas: the ones eligible to become leader without data loss.

hw.committed: The end of committed data (every ISR replica has it)
hw.end: The end of the leader’s log
hw.why: Consumers read up to the HW.

lag.why: 30 000 ms: a follower that hasn’t caught up in 30 s leaves the ISR.

calc.q: The leader has {leader} records, follower A has {a}, follower B has {bb}, and both are in the ISR. What’s the high watermark?

5-3.title: Safety net
5-3.summary: min.insync.replicas: refuse writes rather than risk them.

brief.title: How many copies are enough?
brief.body: acks=all waits for every in-sync replica. But if the ISR shrinks to just the leader, “all” means one copy. min.insync.replicas sets the floor: with fewer replicas in sync, acks=all writes are rejected (NotEnoughReplicas). You trade availability for durability.
brief.breaks: it only applies to producers using acks=all.

alone.title: One copy left
alone.body: With the default min.insync.replicas=1, both followers crash and the producer keeps writing…

net.title: Set the safety net
net.body: Set min.insync.replicas=2 and send an order while only one replica is up: it should be refused (⊘). Then bring back a follower and send again until it’s accepted (✓). (Crash brokers again if you need to.)
net.success: Refused while only one copy existed, accepted once two replicas were in sync. No more “saved” orders that live on a single broker.

one.q: RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, one broker down. acks=all writes…
one.why: Two in-sync replicas meet the floor of 2, so writes go through.

two.q: Same cluster, but two brokers down. acks=all writes…
two.why: Only the leader is in sync, below the floor of 2, so the producer gets an error instead of a fragile “saved”.

default.why: 1. With acks=all that can mean a single copy.

when.q: When does an acks=all write get NotEnoughReplicas?
when.below: When the ISR is smaller than min.insync.replicas

prod.why: It survives one broker loss for writes, and any acknowledged record exists on at least 2 brokers.

acks1.waits: Makes the producer wait for all replicas
acks1.why: The floor is only checked for acks=all.

5-4.title: Who’s in charge?
5-4.summary: KRaft controllers, quorums and leader elections.

brief.title: The control tower
brief.body: Someone has to decide who leads each partition. In Kafka 4.x that’s the KRaft controller quorum: a few controller nodes that keep the cluster’s metadata in a Raft log (__cluster_metadata). One is active, and it runs leader elections. A majority must be alive to do anything.
brief.breaks: ZooKeeper used to do this job. It was removed in Kafka 4.0.

lose.title: Lose a controller
lose.body: Crash the active controller and watch another take over. Then crash a broker that leads a partition: the new active controller should still run the election.
lose.success: The quorum survived one loss (2 of 3 alive) and kept running elections.

noquorum.q: Two of three controllers are down, and then the partition leader dies. What happens?
noquorum.offline: No election: the partition stays offline until a majority is back
noquorum.elected: A new leader is elected anyway
noquorum.why: A single controller is not a majority, so it can’t commit metadata changes and elections stall. That’s why you run 3 (or 5) controllers.

unclean.title: Unclean elections
unclean.body: What if no in-sync replica is alive? By default Kafka waits (the partition is offline). With unclean.leader.election.enable=true, an out-of-sync replica may become leader: the partition is available sooner, but records it never copied are lost. Since Kafka 4.1, Eligible Leader Replicas (ELR) make the safe choice smarter.

choose.q: For orders you can’t afford to lose, unclean.leader.election.enable should be…
choose.why: Waiting for an in-sync replica protects durability. Turn unclean election on only where availability matters more than every record.

job.metadata: Manage cluster metadata and run leader elections
job.why: They handle the control plane. Brokers serve data.

quorum.q: A quorum has {n} controllers. How many can fail while it still works?
quorum.why: It needs a majority ({m} of {n}), so {f} can fail.

unclean.q: Turning on unclean leader election can cause…
unclean.loss: Data loss, in exchange for availability
unclean.why: An out-of-sync leader doesn’t have the latest records.

6-1.title: Diagnose the symptom
6-1.summary: At-most, at-least, exactly-once: match each symptom to its cause.

brief.title: Three promises
brief.body: Every pipeline makes one of three promises. At-most-once: never twice, but maybe never. At-least-once: never lost, but maybe twice. Exactly-once: once, period, which needs extra machinery. Now you’ll play support engineer: each ticket describes a symptom. Which mechanism caused it?
brief.breaks: the mechanisms come from Worlds 3 and 4. They’re mixed on purpose: telling look-alikes apart is what makes the knowledge stick.

s1.q: Ticket: after a short network glitch, some orders appear TWICE in the topic, at different offsets. Cause?
s1.retry: Producer retries after a lost ack, without idempotence
s1.why: Two copies on the log means the producer wrote twice: a retry whose first attempt actually succeeded. enable.idempotence=true fixes it.

s2.q: Ticket: the producer got a success for order #42, but after a broker died, #42 is nowhere in the topic. Cause?
s2.acks1: acks=1: only the leader had it when it died
s2.why: An acknowledged record vanished in a failover, the classic acks=1 loss. Use acks=all (and min.insync.replicas=2).

s3.q: Ticket: after a consumer crash, a few orders were never billed, but they ARE in the topic. Cause?
s3.commitBefore: The consumer committed before processing them
s3.why: The records exist, but the group’s bookmark moved past them before they were handled: at-most-once. Commit after processing.

s4.q: Ticket: after a consumer restart, some customers got TWO invoices for one order (the order is in the topic once). Cause?
s4.autoCommit: The consumer processed records but crashed before committing (auto-commit)
s4.why: One copy on the log but processed twice means consumer-side reprocessing: at-least-once. Make processing idempotent (e.g. dedupe by order id) or use transactions.

s5.q: Ticket: we use Kafka transactions end to end, but customers still sometimes get two confirmation EMAILS. Cause?
s5.sideEffect: Emails are a side effect outside Kafka; transactions can’t roll them back
s5.why: Exactly-once covers reads and writes inside Kafka. An email sent during processing can’t be undone if the transaction aborts and re-runs.

default.q: A typical consumer that commits after processing gives you…
default.why: A crash between processing and committing replays records.

idem.q: The usual way to make at-least-once safe is to…
idem.why: If handling a record twice has the same effect as once, duplicates don’t matter.

6-2.title: All or nothing
6-2.summary: Transactions: markers, read_committed and the last stable offset.

brief.title: An order and its invoice
brief.body: Some writes belong together: an order in orders and its invoice in invoices. A transaction makes them atomic: both become visible, or neither does. The coordinator finishes it by dropping a COMMIT or ABORT marker into every partition it touched. Two readers watch orders: Billing reads read_committed, Audit reads read_uncommitted (the default).

abort.title: Change of plans: abort
abort.body: Begin a transaction, send an order + invoice, then abort it. Compare what Billing and Audit saw.
abort.success: Audit (read_uncommitted) saw the aborted order. Billing (read_committed) never did: aborted records are filtered out.

stuck.q: A transaction is open and not finished yet. What does Billing (read_committed) do at that point in the log?
stuck.waits: Waits: it can’t read past the first open record (the LSO)
stuck.skips: Skips the open records and keeps reading
stuck.why: read_committed stops at the last stable offset until the transaction commits or aborts. A long-open transaction stalls these consumers.

commit.title: Now commit
commit.body: Begin, send an order + invoice, watch Billing wait, then commit. Do it until Billing has received 2 orders.
commit.success: COMMIT dropped in, the LSO moved and Billing caught up. Both topics show the writes together.

atomic.q: A transaction that writes to two topics guarantees…
atomic.all: Both writes become visible, or neither does
atomic.order: The topics stay in the same order
atomic.why: Atomic visibility across partitions and topics.

default.why: The default returns everything, aborted data included. Set read_committed for transactional pipelines.

lso.open: The first offset of a still-open transaction
lso.hw: Always equal to the high watermark
lso.why: read_committed consumers can’t read past it.

markers.q: How does Kafka record that a transaction committed or aborted?
markers.markers: Control markers written into each partition it touched
markers.why: Records are immutable. Markers tell readers how to treat them.

6-3.title: Exactly once, and zombies
6-3.summary: Read-process-write with transactions, and fencing of zombie producers.

brief.title: The exactly-once recipe
brief.body: A processor reads orders and writes invoices. For exactly-once, the invoice writes and the consumer’s offset commit go into the same transaction (sendOffsetsToTransaction). If the processor dies mid-way, the transaction aborts, so neither the invoice nor the offset “happened”, and the retry starts clean. Readers use read_committed.

crash.title: Crash mid-transaction
crash.body: The processor writes invoice #1 inside a transaction and then crashes. A replacement starts with the same transactional.id, fences the old instance, aborts its open transaction and redoes the work. Watch Billing (read_committed) on invoices.

count.q: How many copies of invoice #1 did Billing receive?
count.why: One. The first attempt was aborted and filtered out, the retry committed. The log holds both, but read_committed sees one.

zombie.q: The old processor wakes up (a “zombie”) and tries to commit its transaction. What happens?
zombie.fenced: It’s fenced: the broker rejects it because a newer epoch owns that transactional.id
zombie.duplicate: Its invoice is added, a duplicate
zombie.why: Each new instance bumps the producer epoch for its transactional.id. Requests from older epochs fail with ProducerFenced (strengthened by KIP-890 in 4.0).

email.q: The processor also sends the customer an email when it creates an invoice. With this exactly-once setup, can a customer get two emails?
email.maybe: Yes: the email isn’t part of the Kafka transaction
email.why: Side effects outside Kafka aren’t rolled back. Make them idempotent (dedupe by invoice id) or move them downstream of committed data.

recipe.q: Exactly-once for read-process-write in Kafka uses…
recipe.txn: An idempotent transactional producer + offsets committed in the transaction + read_committed readers

offsets.q: In an exactly-once processor, the consumer offsets are committed…
offsets.inside: Inside the same transaction as the output
offsets.why: sendOffsetsToTransaction ties progress and output together.

zombie.q: How does Kafka stop a zombie producer from committing stale work?
zombie.why: Newer instance, higher epoch: older epochs are rejected.

limits.external: Side effects outside Kafka (databases, emails, APIs)
limits.why: Only Kafka reads and writes are inside the transaction.

7-1.title: Segments
7-1.summary: A partition is a chain of segment files; only the last one is written.

brief.title: A partition is a stack of files
brief.body: On disk, a partition isn’t one endless file. It’s a chain of segments. New records always go to the last one, the active segment. When it reaches segment.bytes (1 GiB) or segment.ms (7 days), it’s closed and a new one starts (a “roll”).
brief.breaks: here a segment holds just 4 parcels so you can watch it roll.

fill.title: Fill the log
fill.body: Ten orders arrive. Watch the dividers: every 4 parcels the active segment closes and a new one opens.

count.q: Segments hold 4 records. After 13 records, how many segments does the partition have?
count.why: Offsets 0–3, 4–7, 8–11 and 12: four segments. The last one is active.

where.why: Segments are append-only files, and only the active one is open for writing.

roll.title: Roll a new segment
roll.body: Send orders until a fourth segment appears.
roll.success: Rolled! The full segment closed, and from now on only retention or compaction will touch it.

count.q: Segments hold {size} records. After {n} records, how many segments are there?

write.why: Only the newest segment is open for writes.

roll.q: By default a segment rolls at…

unit.q: Retention deletes data in units of…
unit.why: That’s why a record can outlive its retention time: its segment must close and expire first.

7-2.title: Out with the old
7-2.summary: Retention deletes whole segments; offsets are never reused.

brief.title: Nothing lasts forever
brief.body: With cleanup.policy=delete, Kafka deletes whole closed segments once they’re older than retention.ms (7 days by default) or the partition exceeds retention.bytes. The first offset still on disk, the log start offset, moves forward. Offsets are never reused.

fill.title: A busy week
fill.body: Eleven orders arrive. Audit read one of the first ones and then went on holiday…

room.title: Make room
room.body: Lower how many segments are kept and watch whole segments disappear. Then send a couple more orders.
room.success: Whole segments vanished at once, and new orders kept counting up from where the log ended.

next.q: After the deletion, what offset will the next order get?
next.why: {end}: offsets keep counting. Deleted numbers are never handed out again.

audit.q: Audit comes back. Its position points at an offset that was deleted. What happens on its next fetch?
audit.reset: OffsetOutOfRange, so it resets according to auto.offset.reset
audit.why: Its position is below the log start. The reset policy decides where it lands (here earliest = the new log start). It silently skipped history: monitor lag before data expires!

whole.each: Each record exactly at its deadline
whole.why: Deletion works per segment, never on the active one.

reuse.q: A partition’s log ended at offset {end} before retention deleted its first segments. What offset does the next record get?

oor.q: A consumer’s position is below the log start offset. Then…
oor.waits: It waits until the data comes back
oor.why: The data is gone. The reset policy picks a new position.

7-3.title: Latest only
7-3.summary: Compaction keeps the latest value per key; tombstones delete keys.

brief.title: An address book, not a diary
brief.body: Some topics hold state: each customer’s current profile. With cleanup.policy=compact, a background cleaner removes records that a newer record with the same key has replaced. A consumer reading from the start still rebuilds the same final state, from far fewer records.
brief.breaks: the cleaner never touches the active segment, and offsets never change: compaction leaves gaps.

updates.title: Profile updates
updates.body: Customers keep updating their profiles: alice three times, bob twice. The table shows the state a consumer would rebuild.

survive.q: The cleaner runs. Which of alice’s records survive?
survive.why: For each key only the newest record is needed to rebuild state. Older versions in closed segments are removed.

offsets.q: After compaction, are the remaining records renumbered?
offsets.gaps: No: offsets stay the same, leaving gaps
offsets.why: Records are immutable and keep their offsets. Consumers just skip the gaps.

forget.title: Forget carol
forget.body: carol asked to be deleted. Write a tombstone for her (key + null value), send a few more updates so it lands in a closed segment, then run the cleaner.
forget.success: carol is gone from the rebuilt state, and her old records were removed. The tombstone itself stays for a while (delete.retention.ms, 1 day) so every consumer sees the deletion.

keeps.latest: At least the latest record for each key
keeps.first: The first record for each key
keeps.why: Older versions of a key can be removed.

tomb.q: How do you delete a key from a compacted topic?
tomb.null: Write a record with that key and a null value (a tombstone)
tomb.delete: Call a delete API on the offset
tomb.why: Tombstones delete the key; they’re cleaned up after delete.retention.ms.

offsets.why: An offset identifies a record forever.

7-4.title: Cold storage
7-4.summary: Tiered storage: old segments move to cheap remote storage and stay readable.

brief.title: The warehouse in the cloud
brief.body: Keeping a year of data on broker disks is expensive. Tiered storage (production-ready since Kafka 3.9) copies closed segments to remote object storage (like S3) and keeps only recent ones on local disk. Consumers don’t notice: the broker fetches old data from remote storage for them.

offload.title: Offloading
offload.body: Ten orders arrive. Only the newest closed segment stays local; older ones turn blue: they now live in remote storage.

read.q: Archive wants to read offset 0, which is now in remote storage. What happens?
read.broker: The broker fetches it from remote storage and serves it
read.s3: Archive must read from S3 itself
read.why: Remote segments are still part of the log. The broker serves them (recent reads still come from local disk).

archive.title: Read the archive
archive.body: Let Archive read the first 4 orders, all from remote segments.
archive.success: Old data, served transparently. Cheap long retention without big broker disks.

compact.q: Can a compacted topic use tiered storage?
compact.why: Tiered storage works with delete-policy topics. Compacted topics stay on local disks.

what.offload: Moves closed segments to remote object storage while keeping them readable

serve.q: Who serves reads of remote segments to consumers?
serve.why: Consumers keep talking to brokers only.

which.why: The active segment is still being written.

compact.q: Do compacted topics support tiered storage?

8-1.title: Pipes from the database
8-1.summary: Kafka Connect copies a database table into a topic and remembers where it stopped.

brief.title: No code, just a pipe
brief.body: Your customers live in a database, and the shop wants them in Kafka. You could write a producer, or plug in Kafka Connect: a framework that runs ready-made connectors. A source connector copies an outside system into topics. A sink connector copies topics out to another system. Workers run each connector as one or more tasks.

map.source: Source system (read by a source connector)

copy.title: Rows become records
copy.body: The task copies each row into db-customers, keyed by its id. Every 3 rows it writes its position to connect-offsets: Connect keeps its own bookmark in a Kafka topic.

resume.q: The task copied 5 rows but only flushed its position after row 3. It crashes. Where does the new task start?
resume.flushed: After row 3, the last flushed position
resume.where: After row 5, where the old task really was
resume.why: A new task only knows what is in connect-offsets. Rows 4 and 5 get copied again: Connect is at-least-once by default. In real Kafka the flush runs every offset.flush.interval.ms (60 s by default).

crash.title: Crash the pipe
crash.body: Add rows to the database, then crash the task before it flushes (look at the line in the table). Restart it and watch it copy some rows twice.
crash.success: Duplicates, exactly as predicted. The bookmark lives in Kafka, so nothing is lost, but some rows may arrive twice.

fix.q: How do you make those re-sent rows harmless downstream?
fix.upsert: Key the records by row id and treat them as upserts
fix.never: You can't; duplicates always break things
fix.why: Each record is keyed by the row id, so a second copy of customer-4 just says the same thing again. Read as a table (upsert by key) or with an idempotent sink, duplicates do no harm. Newer Kafka can also run source connectors exactly-once (KIP-618).

where.q: Where does a source connector keep its position in distributed mode?
where.why: Connect stores source offsets in a Kafka topic, often called connect-offsets, so any worker can pick the task up.

sink.q: A sink connector reads topics using…
sink.why: Sink tasks are consumers in a group, so they get partitions assigned and commit offsets like any consumer.

what.framework: A framework that runs connectors in worker processes
what.plugin: A plugin loaded inside the brokers
what.why: Workers run separately from brokers. Connectors are plugins for Connect, not for the broker.

dups.q: A task flushes its position every {flush} rows. It copied {copied} rows and the last flush was after row {flushed}. It crashes and restarts. How many rows get copied twice?
dups.why: It restarts from row {flushed}, so rows {flushed}+1 to {copied} go out again: {extra}.

8-2.title: Stream or table?
8-2.summary: The same topic read two ways: every event (KStream) or the latest value per key (KTable).

brief.title: A diary and an address book
brief.body: Kafka Streams is a Java library you put inside your own app. It can read a topic two ways. A KStream is every event, like a diary: "alice moved to Lima", "alice moved to Madrid". A KTable keeps only the latest value per key, like an address book. A new record for a key replaces the old one (an upsert).
brief.breaks: it is a library, not a cluster. Your app runs it, and you scale it by starting more copies of your app.

moves.title: People move
moves.body: Five moves arrive. The KStream lists all five. The KTable keeps one row per person.

rows.q: alice, bob, alice, carol, bob moved. How many rows does the KTable have?
rows.why: Three people: alice, bob and carol. The KTable keeps one row per key.

again.q: alice moves again, to Porto. What does the KTable show for alice?
again.why: An upsert: the new record replaces alice's row. The KStream still has all her moves.

delete.title: Delete a row
delete.body: Send a tombstone (a null value) for bob or carol and watch the row disappear from the KTable. Then add dave or erin.
delete.success: A null value means "delete this key" for a table, but the stream still has every event, the tombstone included.

upsert.q: A new record for an existing key in a KTable…
upsert.append: Is added as a second row
upsert.why: A KTable is a changelog view: latest value per key.

null.q: In a KTable, a record with a null value…
null.why: A null value is a tombstone: the key is removed from the table.

rows.q: A topic has {events} records spread over {keys} different keys, with no deletes. How many rows does its KTable have?
rows.why: One row per key: {keys}. The KStream would have all {events}.

library.library: Add the library to your app and run your app
library.why: Kafka Streams is a client library. Scale it by running more instances of your app.

8-3.title: State that survives
8-3.summary: A counting app keeps its state in a local store backed by a changelog topic, and gets it back after a crash.

brief.title: The notebook and its carbon copy
brief.body: Counting clicks per user needs state: the count so far. Kafka Streams keeps it in a local state store (a notebook on the app's own disk). Every change is also written to a changelog topic, a carbon copy in Kafka. If the machine dies, a new instance replays the changelog and gets the notebook back.

count.title: Counting clicks
count.body: Clicks arrive. Each one updates the count in the store, and the new count goes to click-counter-counts-changelog.

crash.q: The machine dies, disk and all. A new instance starts. What is alice's count?
crash.same: The same as before: it's rebuilt from the changelog
crash.never: The app can't start without the old disk
crash.why: The changelog topic has every update, so replaying it rebuilds the store before the app processes new clicks.

restore.title: Crash and restore
restore.body: Crash the app (its store is wiped), restart it and watch it restore from the changelog. Then send a couple more clicks: the counts must keep adding up.
restore.success: Back to the same counts, then on to new clicks. Local speed, with Kafka as the backup.

compact.q: Why is a changelog topic compacted?
compact.latest: Restoring only needs the latest value per key
compact.order: To keep the records in order
compact.why: The store only needs alice's latest count, not every step. Compaction keeps the changelog small, so restores are fast.

where.q: Where does a Kafka Streams app keep a count?
where.both: In a local state store, backed by a changelog topic
where.memory: Only in memory, lost on restart
where.why: Local for speed, changelog for safety.

group.q: A Kafka Streams app uses which consumer group id?
group.why: application.id names the group, the internal topics and the changelog topics.

compact.q: A compacted changelog got {updates} updates for {keys} keys. After compaction, how many records does a restore need at least?
compact.why: Compaction keeps the latest per key: {keys} (of {updates}).

restore.q: To rebuild a lost state store, Kafka Streams replays…
restore.input: The input topic from the beginning
restore.why: The changelog already holds the store's contents, compacted to the latest per key.

8-4.title: Time windows
8-4.summary: Count per 10-second window by event time, and decide how long to wait for late records.

brief.title: Shifts on the clock
brief.body: "Clicks per minute" needs windows. A tumbling window has a fixed size and windows never overlap: [0–10), [10–20)… Each record goes into a window by its event time (its timestamp), not by when it arrives. Records can arrive late, so a window waits a grace period before it closes. Anything later than that is dropped.

map.stamp: The time printed on the ticket
map.late: How long the door stays open

fill.title: Filling windows
fill.body: Clicks happen at 3 s, 6 s, 9 s and 12 s. Stream time is the newest timestamp seen. With grace 0, window [0–10) closes once stream time reaches 10.

late.q: Stream time is 12 s and grace is 0. A click that happened at 7 s arrives now. What happens?
late.dropped: It's dropped: window [0–10) is already closed
late.why: 7 s belongs to [0–10), which closed at 10 + 0 grace. Late records for a closed window are dropped (Kafka Streams logs and counts them).

grace.title: Hold the door
grace.body: Pick a grace period so clicks 5 s late still count, then send a click 15 s late and see it dropped.
grace.success: Grace is a trade-off: more of the late data gets counted, but final results arrive later.

hour.q: Why not just set the grace period to an hour?
hour.wait: Windows stay open longer: final results come later and more state is kept
hour.why: A long grace catches more late data, but every window waits that long to be final, and its state is kept the whole time.

kind.q: Windows of a fixed size that never overlap are…
kind.why: Hopping windows overlap (they advance by less than their size). Session windows grow with activity.

start.q: Tumbling windows of {size} s. A record has event time {ts} s. At what second does its window start?

close.q: Window [{start}–{end}) has a grace period of {grace} s. At what stream time does it close?
close.why: End + grace: {end} + {grace} = {close}. Records for it after that are dropped.

time.q: Which time decides a record's window?
time.why: Windows use event time, which is why late arrivals are possible and need a grace period.

9-1.title: More robots than belts
9-1.summary: A classic group can't use more consumers than partitions. A share group can.

brief.title: A queue, Kafka style
brief.body: In a classic consumer group each partition belongs to one member, so with 2 partitions a third and fourth consumer just wait. Sometimes you only want "a pile of jobs, any free worker takes the next one": a queue. Kafka 4 adds share groups (KIP-932) for that. Members take records from the same partitions together, so there can be more workers than partitions.

map.next: Any free robot grabs the next parcel

classic.title: Two robots, twiddling thumbs
classic.body: Four robots, two belts, a classic group: each belt has one owner and the other two robots say zzz.

idle.q: 4 robots, 2 belts, classic group. How many robots sit idle?
idle.why: One owner per partition: 2 work, 2 wait. Adding consumers beyond the partition count doesn't help a classic group.

switch.title: Everyone to work
switch.body: Switch the group type to share and watch all four robots grab jobs. Get throughput above 3.4 jobs per second.
switch.success: Four workers on two partitions. Share groups make Kafka a work queue as well as a log.

order.q: Does a share group process each customer's records in order?
order.no: No: records are handed to whichever worker is free
order.why: Order is the price: many workers pick from the same partition at once. Use a classic group when per-key order matters.

idle.q: A classic group has {members} members on a topic with {parts} partitions. How many members are idle?
idle.why: One member per partition at most: {members} − {parts} = {idle} idle.

order.q: A share group guarantees per-key ordering…
order.why: Records go to whichever member is free, so there's no ordering guarantee.

when.q: When is a share group the right tool?
when.queue: Independent jobs where any worker can take the next one
when.ordered: Bank transactions that must stay in order per account
when.replay: Rebuilding a table by replaying a compacted topic
when.why: Queue-style work: more workers than partitions, order not needed.

class.q: Which Java client class reads from a share group?
class.why: Share groups have their own client, KafkaShareConsumer.

9-2.title: Locks and retries
9-2.summary: Each record is locked while a worker has it. Accept, release or reject it; a poison record gets archived.

brief.title: A timer on every parcel
brief.body: In a share group, a worker acquires a record with a lock (30 s by default). When it's done it acknowledges: ACCEPT (processed), RELEASE (put it back for another try) or REJECT (it can never be processed). If the worker dies, the lock runs out and the record becomes available again. Each try adds to the delivery count; at the limit (5) the record is archived.

crash.title: A robot drops the parcel
crash.body: A robot crashes while holding a job. Nobody can take that job until its lock runs out; then it is delivered again (the red badge counts tries).

poison.q: A corrupt file fails every time and the worker RELEASEs it. The limit is 5 deliveries. What happens?
poison.archived: After the 5th try it is archived and skipped
poison.why: The delivery limit stops poison records: after 5 deliveries the record is archived and the workers move on.

reject.title: Don't retry the hopeless
reject.body: Corrupt PDFs (☠) arrive every few seconds. Releasing them wastes 5 tries each. Switch failures to reject so they're archived on the first try, and keep finishing the good jobs.
reject.success: REJECT for things that can never work, RELEASE for things that might work later.

lock.q: A worker crashes holding a record. When can another worker get it?
lock.why: The broker waits for the lock to run out (group.share.record.lock.duration.ms), then makes the record available again.

reject.q: A record can never be processed (corrupt data). Which acknowledgement?
reject.why: REJECT archives it right away; RELEASE would just retry it.

crash.q: A share consumer crashes while holding records. They become available again…
crash.why: The acquisition lock protects the record until it times out.

left.q: A record has been delivered {done} times and the limit is {limit}. How many more deliveries can it get?

release.again: Goes back and will be delivered again
release.why: RELEASE makes it available again (and the delivery count grows).

9-3.title: Why Kafka is fast
9-3.summary: Appending to files, the OS page cache, zero-copy and batching. And what TLS costs.

brief.title: Tricks of a fast warehouse
brief.body: Kafka doesn't jump around the disk: it only appends to the end of log files, which disks are very good at. It leaves caching to the operating system's page cache. When a consumer reads, the broker can send bytes straight from the page cache to the network (zero-copy, sendfile) without copying them through the JVM. And everything travels in batches.

map.notebook: Writing on the next line of a notebook
map.chute: A chute from shelf to truck
map.truck: A full truck, not one parcel at a time

gap.q: On the same disks, how much faster are sequential (append) writes than random writes?
gap.why: Kafka's design docs measured about 600 MB/s linear versus about 100 kB/s random on the same disks. That's why Kafka only appends.

max.title: Full speed
max.body: Turn the dials until the broker pushes at least 500 MB/s. Watch the belt fill as throughput rises.
max.success: Append-only writes, zero-copy and big batches: that's the recipe.

tls.q: Your security team turns on TLS. What happens to zero-copy?
tls.off: It switches off: the bytes must be encrypted in the JVM first
tls.why: sendfile can't encrypt, so with TLS the broker copies data into the JVM to encrypt it. Still fast, just not zero-copy.

secure.title: TLS is mandatory
secure.body: Turn on TLS and get the best throughput you still can (at least 300 MB/s).
secure.success: TLS costs zero-copy, but sequential writes and batching still carry most of the speed.

seq.q: How does Kafka write to disk?
seq.append: It appends to the end of log files
seq.index: It updates records in place by key
seq.memory: It keeps everything in heap memory
seq.why: Sequential appends are what disks do best.

zero.q: With zero-copy, the broker sends data from the page cache straight to…
zero.why: sendfile skips the copy into the application.

tls.why: Encryption happens in the JVM, so the data must be copied there.

cache.q: Which cache does Kafka lean on for recent data?
cache.heap: A big cache in the JVM heap
cache.none: None, it always reads the disk
cache.why: The page cache keeps recent log data in memory without bloating the JVM.

9-4.title: The noisy neighbour
9-4.summary: One client hogs the broker. A quota throttles it so everyone gets their share.

brief.title: One greedy client
brief.body: Brokers are shared. If one client (here, a batch analytics job) pushes as fast as it can, the others slow down. Quotas cap a client's bytes per second (producer_byte_rate, consumer_byte_rate) per user or client id. Over the limit, the broker doesn't drop anything: it throttles the client by delaying its responses.

map.limit: A speed limit for one truck company

look.title: Watch the flood
look.body: The broker handles 100 MB/s. Orders needs 50, analytics pushes 200. Watch who gets what.
look.success: Analytics takes most of the broker and orders crawls at 20 MB/s.

how.q: How does a broker enforce a quota?
how.why: The broker computes a throttle time and holds the response, so the client slows down by itself. Nothing is lost.

cap.title: Give orders room
cap.body: Set a quota on the analytics client so orders gets its 50 MB/s.
cap.success: Analytics is throttled (see the throttle time), orders flows again, and nobody lost data.

sees.q: What does the analytics producer notice when it is throttled?
sees.slower: Its sends take longer (throttle time in its metrics)
sees.why: Throttled clients just go slower. The throttle time shows up in client metrics.

how.q: Over its quota, a client is…
how.why: Throttling slows the client down; no data is dropped.

who.why: Quotas target who is sending or reading: users and client ids.

bytes.q: producer_byte_rate is in bytes per second. What value means {mb} MiB/s?

sees.why: Fetch responses are delayed; the records are all still there.
